analysis.one_liner: Shields countertop stone makers and sellers from silicosis lawsuits by fabrication workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sue makers, importers, and sellers of engineered stone slabs — the countertop material that releases lung-destroying silica dust when cut — for illnesses caused by that dust. It would also wipe out lawsuits already in court. The bill says the companies have no control over the cutting shops where workers get sick; critics would say the companies profit from a product whose dust causes the disease. As of now it has not moved: no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers of quartz and other stone slabs. They would be permanently immune from silicosis lawsuits, including suits already filed, shifting the entire cost of a fatal lung disease off the companies that sell the material.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Stone slab makers, importers, and sellers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any civil action in federal or state court against a manufacturer or seller of a stone slab product for injuries from silica dust or other substances released when a third party fabricates the product [S2][S3].
Requires every such lawsuit already pending on the date of enactment to be dismissed, wiping out existing claims [S2][S3].
Covers sellers broadly — importers, distributors, retailers, and suppliers are all shielded, and the shield extends to slabs made of quartz, glass, porcelain, ceramic, and similar materials [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Countertop fabrication workers — disproportionately immigrant workers in small shops — who develop silicosis, an incurable and often fatal lung disease, along with their families and the insurers or public programs that end up covering their care. The bill leaves those workers with no legal claim against the companies whose product generates the dust.
analysis.who_pays_short: Silica-exposed fabrication workers and their families

drawbacks.text: It eliminates the main accountability tool for a deadly occupational disease: workers could no longer sue the companies that profit from selling the material whose cutting causes silicosis, leaving only enforcement of workplace safety rules against the small shops doing the cutting [S3].
It applies retroactively, dismissing lawsuits that are already pending, which strips away claims workers have already brought [S3].
By making fabricators the only remaining defendants, it concentrates all liability on small fabrication businesses while immunizing the large manufacturers and importers upstream [S3].

The bill's own argument — that fabricators are regulated by OSHA silica rules and that manufacturers have no control over them — acknowledges the mechanism but does not address that regulation prevents neither exposure nor disease [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry case is real: manufacturers don't run the cutting shops, and fabricators who ignore safety rules are the direct cause of exposure. But silicosis is incurable, the dust comes from the product the manufacturers sell, and lawsuits are the main pressure that pushes the industry toward safer materials or practices. This bill removes that pressure entirely while leaving sick workers uncompensated — a large benefit to a concentrated industry paid for by the people most injured by its product.

outcome.mechanism: It's sitting in the Senate Judiciary Committee; nobody has cosponsored it and no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Ashley Moody introduced the bill in the Senate on June 16, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
No senator has cosponsored it; the cosponsor list is empty [S4].

The bill would prohibit civil actions against manufacturers and sellers of stone slab products for silicosis and related conditions caused by silica dust generated during fabrication by third parties, and would dismiss any such action pending at enactment [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: the stone slab industry's immunity is not yet law, and workers' existing silicosis lawsuits are still alive. The status quo, which the bill would upend, currently favors the workers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Stone slab makers; workers' suits still alive

for.name: Sen. Ashley Moody
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee; no colleagues joined as cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has been taken and no one has publicly opposed it in the record; the only recorded action is the introduction and committee referral [S5].

industries.industry: Engineered stone and stone slab manufacturers, importers, and sellers
industries.note: The bill hands this industry a litigation shield for silicosis claims arising from its product, including suits already in court. Its gain comes directly at the cost of workers sickened by silica dust, who would lose their only claim against the companies that sell the material.

Fabricators are not shielded, so they would remain the only parties who can be sued for silicosis, concentrating liability on smaller businesses that do the cutting. Workers at those shops would get no new protection from the bill either.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys handling silicosis and toxic tort cases
industries.note: A whole category of silica litigation would be barred by statute, and pending cases dismissed, removing the fee-generating cases along with the remedy for workers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors and no committee action rarely reach the floor; unless the sponsor recruits cosponsors or the committee schedules a hearing, this bill most likely dies at the end of the Congress without a vote.
